name: Kashmir
lede: Kashmir is a dark, muted green named for the Himalayan valley; nothing in the books explains why, though the place is famous for shawls, saffron and sapphires.

sections.title: Name and meaning
sections.body:
*Kashmir* is a place name used as a color name for a muted, dark green. It is the name of the mountain valley and region in the Himalayas, and the color is filed in our sources as a place word, with no record of why this green carries it [1]. The earliest record is Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930, where it appears on plate 30, block E8, with a first use given as 1925 [1]. Who chose the name is undocumented.

That matters because the place is much better known for other colors. Paterson's dictionary lists "Kashmir blues" in a set of evocative regional phrases, with Rajasthan reds and Topkapi greens [2]. The green on this page is not one of those [1][2].

sections.title: The shawl colors
sections.body:
The color most often attached to Kashmir in the books is cloth [3]. Finlay follows the Kashmir shawl, woven from fine pashm goat wool, through a history that runs from legend to ledger [3]. One tradition dates a loom technique to the eleventh century, and other scholars dispute that date; by the fifteenth century, a century after the valley's conversion to Islam, a distinct technique had emerged [3]. One legend has the eighth sultan, whose reign ran from 1418 to 1470, calling in a Turkestan weaver to adapt it [3].

Color changed after Emperor Jahangir first spent a spring in the valley in 1620 and wrote of its tulips [4]. Court painters were already copying European botanical pictures, and from then the shawls turned from stylized, geometric flowers toward naturalistic ones [4]. Fragments in the Victoria and Albert Museum are described by conservators with a color list: peony red, verdigris and cinnamon on vanilla, or straw, saxe blue, green muscat, claret and mole on a saffron ground [5].

Those shawls were soft, not hard-edged: in the twill tapestry technique one color slides into the next, so the pattern seems to float [5]. Owen Jones, in his *Grammar of Ornament* of 1856, held up the Kashmir shawl as an example of colors that blend to a neutral bloom at a distance and reveal detail close up [6]. Indigo ran through the cloth as well. Balfour-Paul notes that late eighteenth-century shawls contain yarns dyed with sulphonated indigo, the bright turquoise-leaning "Saxon blue" invented around 1740 [7], and that indigo-and-white striped bier cloths were woven in Kashmir for Syria in the same century [8].

sections.title: Saffron and the sapphire
sections.body:
Two other things carry the place name to the color world. The first is saffron: the spice has been grown in Kashmir since at least 500 BC by Finlay's account, though she judges the local claim that saffron was born there to be probably wrong [9]. When she went looking for the saffron harvest, the industry in Kashmir had shrunk to under a ton a year [9]. Monastic robes in Tibet, often called saffron, are not dyed with it [9].

The second is the Kashmir sapphire, a gem that shares with the best Golconda diamonds a liveliness the trade calls "fine water" [10]. Its nearest visual match today is not a sapphire at all but [[gem:tanzanite|tanzanite]], discovered in 1967 [10]. Neither is the green shown here [10].

sections.title: The swatch is not the history
sections.body:
The swatch is `#426C53`, ISCC-NBS "moderate green", within CIEDE2000 5.6 of the block center, with a Munsell reading of about 2.9G 4.1/4 [1]. It is dark and quiet, with lightness under half and low chroma [1]. Nearby named colors in our data include [[viridian]], 10.6 units away, and [[hunter-green]], 8.8 units away [1].

No passage in our books ties this green to a Kashmir dye, shawl or stone [1][2]. Treat it as a name borrowed for its mountain-valley feeling, not as a product of the place [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 168 contain this swatch, which is 0.71 percent, as photographed, and it is more common than 56 percent of the named colors [11]. Inside a painting it most often plays a shadow, in 30 percent of the 83 paintings where we can measure it [11].

The painter who leans on it most is [[painter:paul-cezanne|Cézanne]], with the color in 7 of his 50 works in the archive, 8.4 times the rate of the museums they come from [11]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 1.3 percent of the 1,674 paintings from then, 3.3 times the expected rate, and it is most over-represented in France, at 2.4 times [11]. The earliest dated match is a painting from 1480, but the early centuries are thin, so that is a floor, not a first [11]. A match is a look-alike hue in an aged, varnished photograph, not proof of any pigment [11].
